identity.title: All-Purpose Mean Estimation over R: Optimal Sub-Gaussianity with Outlier Robustness and Low Moments Performance

problem.claim: Design a one-dimensional mean estimator usable across standard, contaminated, and heavy-tailed settings while retaining optimal standard-setting performance.

gap.claim: The Lee–Valiant estimator had standard finite-variance optimality but lacked proven guarantees under adversarial corruption and infinite-variance heavy tails.

contributions.claim: Shows the Lee–Valiant estimator tolerates strong contamination and achieves stated optimal rates for finite-variance corruption and finite z-th moments with z in (1,2).
Shows that outlier robustness implies neighborhood optimality for one-dimensional estimators that are simultaneously robust and sub-Gaussian.
Establishes asymptotic normality and efficiency for the Lee–Valiant estimator.

stated_novelty.claim: Extends neighborhood-optimality guarantees beyond median-of-means to all estimators that are both robust and sub-Gaussian, resolving a question attributed to Dang et al.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report an O(σ√η) estimation error under an η-fraction of strong contamination for variance-σ² distributions.
The authors report finite-z-moment performance matching Devroye et al.'s lower bounds up to constants for z in (1,2).
The authors report asymptotic normality and efficiency of the Lee–Valiant estimator.

narrative_sequence.summary: Introduces all-purpose one-dimensional mean estimation and prior standard-setting optimality of the Lee–Valiant estimator.
Identifies missing robustness guarantees under strong contamination and infinite-variance heavy tails, then asks whether robustness can coexist with standard optimality.
Reports contamination robustness, optimal finite-variance and low-moment error, and a robustness-to-neighborhood-optimality implication.
Reports asymptotic normality and efficiency as further cross-setting performance evidence.

source_observation.claim: The abstract organizes one estimator's claim around distinct regimes—standard variance, contamination, low moments, neighborhood optimality, and asymptotics—with explicit rates or comparison targets where available.

lessons.interpretation: A multi-regime claim is easier to assess when each regime has its own guarantee or benchmark.
lessons.application: When presenting a broadly applicable method, partition the abstract by operating regime and attach a concrete rate, lower-bound comparison, or asymptotic property to each.
lessons.exception: This structure is unsuitable when the method is intentionally specialized to one regime or when regime-specific guarantees are unavailable.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify sample-size dependence, constants, estimator details, theorem assumptions beyond the named settings, or how asymptotic efficiency is defined.
The abstract does not provide experimental results or details supporting the reported theoretical claims.
